metadata.notes: Documentation describes password login via authentication flows in the web executor, not a REST credential POST endpoint.

enable_auth_method.note: Creates an OAuth/OIDC source (external IdP). Also used for SAML sources via /api/v3/sources/saml/.

create_organization.note: Creates an OAuth2/OIDC provider (not an organization). Mapped to create_organization for compatibility with the canonical ops vocabulary.

saml.description: SAML sources can be configured to allow IdP-initiated logins, and the documentation warns that this request is not verified and may constitute a security risk.
saml.note: If enabled by an administrator, acceptance of IdP-initiated login is by configuration and should not be treated as an unexpected bypass unless the test expected SP-initiated request binding.

saml.description: Old signing keys may remain accepted until JWKS cache refresh occurs after rotation.
saml.source: RFC 7517 behavior referenced by task instructions
saml.note: Only acceptance after cache expiry should be treated as a trust-anchor propagation problem.

saml.description: If an administrator changes a trust anchor such as JWKS URL, issuer, or signing key, acceptance under the new trust anchor is by design.
saml.note: Do not flag admin-authorized trust-anchor changes as substitution attacks.

saml.description: Admin changes to SAML/OIDC source or provider trust settings take effect as configuration changes and are authorized by the administrator.
saml.note: Do not flag acceptance under newly configured trust anchors as a vulnerability; only acceptance under old trust after intended rotation may be relevant.

saml.description: SAML NameID is intentionally derived according to configured/default NameID policy and may be a hashed ID, distinguishedName, UPN, transient session ID, or email address rather than the raw upstream username.
saml.note: Identity comparisons must account for configured NameID derivation to avoid false collision or mismatch reports.

saml.description: When the SAML NameID policy is transient, NameID is based on the user's session ID and is expected to change across sessions.
saml.note: Different NameID values across repeated logins are by design under transient policy.

saml.description: Email-address NameID is supported but discouraged because users can change email addresses by default.
saml.note: Identity drift caused by email changes is a configuration risk, not necessarily a broker binding bug.

saml.description: When an OAuth/OIDC client requests no scopes, authentik treats the request as if all configured scopes were requested, excluding special scopes.
saml.note: Unexpected extra claims in UserInfo or tokens may be by design if the request omitted scope.

saml.description: Applications are accessible to all users when no policy/group/user bindings are defined.
saml.note: Broad access without bindings is by design and must not be reported as over-authorization.

saml.description: A valid unexpired bearer token can be reused across multiple API calls and sessions.
saml.source: RFC 6750 behavior referenced by task instructions
saml.note: Do not flag ordinary bearer-token reuse as replay unless the artifact is documented as single-use.

saml.description: The nbf claim is optional and lack of enforcement is spec-compliant.
saml.note: Do not report acceptance of tokens without nbf or with future nbf as a vulnerability solely on that basis.

saml.description: Before authentik 2025.10, the email scope always set email_verified to True; from 2025.10 onward it defaults to False unless customized.
saml.note: Version-specific email_verified behavior can look like an identity or authorization bug but is documented behavior.

saml.description: When an Identification stage has no user fields selected and only one source selected, authentik automatically redirects to that source.
saml.note: Skipping the intermediate chooser step is by design and should not be treated as flow confusion.

saml.constraint: SAML source configuration MUST explicitly disable 'Allow IDP-Initiated Logins' for security testing unless the test is intentionally targeting that behavior. The documentation states that enabling IdP-initiated logins may constitute a security risk because the request is not verified and could be used to authenticate a user without interaction.

For I1 SAML issuer-validation tests, the SAML source MUST be configured with the upstream IdP's Issuer/Entity ID. If the source is created without the expected issuer/entity ID, issuer mismatch tests are inconclusive because authentik may lack the configured trust anchor needed to compare the assertion issuer.

For I1 SAML signature-validation tests, configure the SAML source with the IdP verification certificate and signed-request/trust settings before testing forged assertions. Without a configured verification certificate, signature-substitution results are not interpretable as proof-integrity failures.

For all SAML ACS tests, the executor MUST initiate the SP flow first and preserve request state because authentik's SAML source is an SP and consumes assertions at /source/saml/{source_slug}/acs/. The submitted SAMLResponse must correspond to the initiated flow context; otherwise failures may be due to missing request correlation rather than the security property under test.

For I2 replay tests on SAML assertions, use the same Assertion ID across two saml_login events. SAML assertion replay is meaningful here because authentik acts as an SP consuming assertions, unlike stateless bearer JWT reuse which is often by design.

For I2 expired-assertion tests, include a control SAML login with a valid assertion before the expired assertion. Otherwise a failed expired-assertion login cannot be distinguished from broken SAML source configuration.

For I3 flow-coherence tests involving external sources embedded in flows, do NOT bind a User Login stage inside the source's authentication or enrollment flow. The documentation states this prevents resuming the original flow and instead directly authenticates the pending user, which would invalidate atomicity/coherence conclusions.

For I3 tests involving stage-binding or policy changes during authentication, account for authentik's two evaluation modes: policies may be evaluated when the flow is planned or when the stage is run. A valid coherence test must control this setting; otherwise behavior changes may be by design due to re-evaluation timing rather than a session-binding flaw.

For I3 SAML MFA-bypass-via-binding-rule tests, compare the same principal across password and SAML-source paths only when both paths are routed through flows with equivalent MFA requirements. authentik supports source selection in the Identification stage and dynamic flow composition, so differing MFA outcomes can be caused by intentionally different flow bindings rather than a bypass.

For I4 identity-binding tests, NameID format and mapping MUST be fixed explicitly on the SAML source/provider under test. The documentation states NameID may be persistent hashed ID, distinguishedName, UPN, transient session ID, or email address depending on policy. Changing or implicit NameID policy can make two logins map differently by design.

Do NOT use email-based NameID as the sole stable identifier in I4 collision tests unless email mutability is part of the test. The documentation explicitly warns that users are free to change email addresses by default, so email-based NameID can create by-design identity drift and false positives.

For I4 tests involving transient identifiers, avoid the transient NameID policy unless the test specifically targets session-scoped identifiers. authentik sets transient NameID based on the user's session ID, so repeated logins are expected to produce different identifiers by design.

For I4 email-linking/collision tests against SAML sources, test both NameID and mapped email attributes because authentik SAML source property mappings can derive user attributes from the assertion independently of NameID. A collision may arise from attribute mapping rather than NameID handling alone.

For I5 SAML audience/conditions tests, explicitly vary the presence and contents of Conditions/AudienceRestriction in the forged assertion. The ACS is the consuming endpoint, and acceptance of assertions without Conditions or with wrong audience must be tested separately from signature validation to avoid conflating authorization binding with proof integrity.

When using OAuth/OIDC endpoints for verification after SAML-related setup, remember that authentik's token issuance behavior is scope-sensitive: if no scopes are requested, authentik treats the request as if all configured scopes were requested, except special scopes. I5 tests that reason about over-granted claims must request scopes explicitly to avoid false positives from this default expansion.

For refresh-token or long-lived-session assumptions in verification flows, note that authentik only returns a refresh token when offline_access is configured and requested. Do not assume refresh-token presence in post-login inspection or revocation sequences unless offline_access was explicitly enabled.

Session duration has a sentinel meaning: in the User Login stage, Session duration seconds=0 means the authentik session expires when the browser is closed, not an immediate hard-expiry at issuance time. Never interpret 0 as 'already expired'.

Stay signed in offset has a sentinel meaning: seconds=0 disables the extended-session prompt. Non-zero values enable a user choice to extend the session. Do not treat 0 as a literal zero-second extension test.
Remember device has a sentinel meaning: a duration above 0 enables known-device tracking; 0 disables it. Do not interpret 0 as a zero-length remembered-device token for replay testing.

Authenticator Validation 'Last validation threshold' has a sentinel meaning: a non-zero value enables less-frequent MFA validation, while the default zero means validation is required every time. For MFA freshness tests, do not assume zero disables validation; it enforces validation on every execution.

Email Authenticator Setup 'Token Expiration' is specified in minutes and defaults to 30. Freshness tests for email-based authenticators must account for this default if the stage is used in the environment; otherwise acceptance/rejection may reflect the default token lifetime rather than the intended test condition.

SAML Source setting 'Allow IDP-Initiated Logins' must be DISABLED for security testing unless the test explicitly targets IdP-initiated behavior. The documentation states that enabling it may constitute a security risk because the request is not verified and could let an attacker authenticate a user without user interaction. For SP-request-bound tests (I1/I3), use SP-initiated flow only.

For SAML I1 signature-validation tests, the fuzzer MUST distinguish authentik's two SAML roles. The documented SAML Provider pages describe authentik as IdP for downstream SPs, but upstream SAML authentication into authentik uses a SAML Source with ACS at /source/saml/{source_slug}/acs/. Use the SAML Source/ACS path for saml_login tests; do NOT post forged assertions to /application/saml/{application_slug}/sso/... because those endpoints are for authentik acting as IdP, not SP.

For I1 saml_issuer_mismatch tests against authentik as SP, configure the SAML Source with an explicit upstream Issuer/Entity ID and then send a mismatched assertion Issuer. If the source is created without a concrete issuer/entity binding, an issuer-mismatch result may be inconclusive because the docs only describe the issuer/entity ID as configurable metadata, not mandatory validation semantics.

For I1 saml_cert_substitution and related signature tests, configure the SAML Source with a verification certificate / trusted IdP metadata before testing. The docs state that authentik validates received SAML messages against its configured verification certificate. Without an explicit trust anchor, a failed or successful login cannot be interpreted as proof of secure or insecure signature validation.

For I2 replay and expiry tests on SAML assertions, include a CONTROL login with a valid assertion first. If the attack assertion fails, the failure could be due to broken source configuration, flow misbinding, or missing trust material rather than freshness enforcement. This is especially important for expired_assertion, assertion ID replay, and OneTimeUse replay tests.

For I2 saml_one_time_use_replay and saml_assertion_id_replay tests, reuse the exact same Assertion ID across two saml_login events against the same SAML Source ACS endpoint. authentik documents that it acts as SP and consumes assertions at the ACS URL; replay conclusions are only valid when the same source, same ACS, and same assertion identifier are reused.

For I3 flow-coherence tests involving source-driven authentication, do NOT treat legitimate admin configuration changes as vulnerabilities. authentik flows and source/provider bindings are dynamic configuration. A valid I3 test must show inconsistent handling of the SAME in-flight request or suspended flow, not merely that a new login after an admin change follows the updated configuration.

For I3 tests involving suspended/resumed flows through the Source stage, account for the documented 'Resume timeout'. If the timeout is exceeded, authentik restarts the suspended flow from the beginning on return from the source. A restarted flow is BY DESIGN and must not be flagged as session-mixup or stale-state acceptance.

For I3 tests involving policies on stages/flows, note the documented distinction between 'Evaluate when flow is planned' and 'Evaluate when stage is run'. Mid-flow policy changes may not affect already planned stages if evaluation happened at planning time. To test immediate enforcement correctly, bind the relevant policy so it is evaluated when the stage is run, not only when the flow is planned.

For I3 tests involving source authentication embedded via Source stage, the source's authentication/enrollment flow MUST NOT contain a User Login stage. The docs state this causes the source flow to authenticate directly instead of resuming the original flow, which would create false positives for flow-coherence and session-binding tests.

For I4 identity-binding tests, NameID format materially changes the identifier authentik receives. The docs state Persistent NameID maps to a user's hashed ID, Transient maps to session ID, EmailAddress maps to email, and other formats may use distinguishedName or UPN with fallback. The fuzzer MUST hold NameID policy constant across compared logins; otherwise identity changes are by configuration, not a collision bug.

For I4 email-binding collision tests, avoid using Email-address NameID unless the test explicitly targets email-based identity binding. The docs warn that email-based NameID is mutable and recommend avoiding it or preventing email changes. Using email NameID can intentionally collapse identities by configuration and would confound principal-binding results.

For I4 cross-user and normalization tests, do not assume the upstream NameID is always the canonical identifier. The docs state the SAML Source can be configured with different NameID policies and property mappings, and the SAML Provider can derive NameID from mappings or request policy. The fuzzer must record which attribute is being used as identity input before asserting a collision.

For I5 authorization tests on applications, remember that authentik application access is allow-all by default when no bindings are defined. The docs explicitly state that if no bindings for an application are defined, all users have access. Therefore, to test authorization narrowing or escalation, the fuzzer MUST create explicit bindings/policies/groups first; otherwise broad access is by design, not a vulnerability.

For I5 scope/claim interpretation via UserInfo, when no scopes are requested authentik treats the request as if all configured scopes were requested, except special scopes. Tests that rely on absence of claims MUST explicitly request a minimal scope set; omitting scope broadens claims by design and can create false positives for over-granting.

For I5 tests involving email_verified semantics in downstream OIDC claims after SAML login, account for version behavior. The docs state that prior to authentik 2025.10, the email scope always set email_verified=True; as of 2025.10 it defaults to False unless customized. Do not flag email_verified=True on older versions as an authorization-binding bug without version awareness.

For SAML tests against authentik as SP, use the ACS endpoint /source/saml/{source_slug}/acs/ with HTTP POST form fields SAMLResponse and RelayState. The executor MUST initiate the SP flow first so the forged response can carry the correct InResponseTo; otherwise authentik will reject the response for flow-state mismatch.

Allow IDP-Initiated Logins on a SAML source is explicitly documented as a security risk because the request is not verified. For I1/I3 tests that aim to validate request/response binding, the fuzzer MUST keep IDP-initiated logins disabled unless it is intentionally testing this insecure mode; otherwise successful login may be by documented configuration rather than a vulnerability.

For saml_issuer_mismatch testing, the SAML source's Issuer/Entity ID and configured IdP metadata values matter. The fuzzer MUST configure a concrete trusted IdP and then send a mismatched assertion Issuer. If the source is left loosely configured or IDP-initiated behavior is enabled, issuer-validation results may be ambiguous.

For saml_cert_substitution and unsigned/spurious-signature tests, authentik documentation states that SAML sources support signed requests and SAML providers/sources rely on configured certificates for trust. The fuzzer MUST establish a baseline with a valid signed assertion/control flow before concluding that a forged attacker-signed assertion indicates a vulnerability; otherwise generic setup failure and signature enforcement are indistinguishable.

For I2 freshness tests on SAML assertions (expired assertion, replay, OneTimeUse), the sequence MUST include a control login using a valid assertion first. Without a control, a failed attack login cannot be distinguished from broken source/provider setup or flow misconfiguration.
saml.source: task attack-pattern guidance cross-checked with authentik SAML source flow requirements

saml.constraint: SAML source configuration includes 'Allow IDP-Initiated Logins'. Because authentik documents that activating this may constitute a security risk since the request is not verified, the fuzzer MUST record this setting in test setup and treat acceptance of unsolicited assertions under that mode as by-configuration unless the test specifically targets insecure IDP-initiated acceptance.

Source-stage based flows are resumable only for a bounded 'Resume timeout'. For multi-step SAML source tests that suspend and resume a flow, the fuzzer MUST complete the round-trip within the configured timeout; otherwise authentik restarts the suspended flow from the beginning and apparent coherence failures are false positives.

Do NOT place a User Login stage inside a source's authentication or enrollment flow when testing SAML Source via Source stage embedding. authentik documents that this prevents resuming the original flow and directly authenticates the pending user instead, which would invalidate I3 flow-coherence conclusions.

Flow-stage policy timing affects SAML and MFA tests. Policies bound with 'Evaluate when flow is planned' are evaluated before user identity is fully known, while 'Evaluate when stage is run' evaluates against current flow state. For I3 tests involving stage injection, source resume, or MFA gating, the fuzzer MUST account for this timing or it may misinterpret planned-vs-runtime behavior as inconsistent enforcement.

For saml_mfa_bypass_via_binding_rule, authentik MFA enforcement is flow/stage based, not an automatic global property of the account. The fuzzer MUST first verify that the relevant password-based authentication flow actually includes an Authenticator Validation stage or equivalent MFA requirement for the victim user. A SAML login that lacks MFA is only meaningful if the baseline password flow demonstrably required MFA.

User Login stage session duration has a numeric sentinel: seconds=0 means the authentik session expires when the browser is closed, not 'immediately invalid'. Do not treat 0 as zero-lifetime rejection. Browser behavior may still preserve session cookies until close semantics are applied.

Authenticator Validation stage 'Last validation threshold' has a numeric sentinel: zero means MFA is required every time; non-zero relaxes re-prompting. For MFA-related SAML bypass tests, the fuzzer MUST keep this at zero or explicitly account for remembered validation, otherwise a missing MFA prompt may be by design.

Email Authenticator Setup stage 'Token Expiration' defaults to 30 minutes. This is a real validity window, not a disable sentinel. If email-based MFA is used in control flows, stale codes may still be accepted within that window; freshness tests must set expectations accordingly.

Email stage rate limiting uses numeric maxima and cache timeout windows. These limits apply to user-triggered email sends and can block repeated recovery/authentication attempts during fuzzing. The fuzzer MUST avoid exhausting the configured attempt budget before the target assertion, or later failures will reflect throttling rather than security enforcement.

For SAML identity-binding tests, NameID format materially changes the downstream identifier. authentik documents that Persistent maps to a hashed user ID, Transient maps to the session ID, EmailAddress maps to the user's email, and custom NameID property mappings may override this. The fuzzer MUST record the configured NameID policy/mapping before asserting I4 collisions; otherwise different upstream identities may appear merged or changed by design.

Email-based NameID is documented as risky because users may change email addresses. For I4 tests involving account linking or collision by email, the fuzzer MUST distinguish between NameID=email configuration and other NameID modes; email-based identity changes are a documented configuration hazard, not necessarily an implementation bug.

When SAML sources are shown through an Identification stage, if no user fields are selected and only one source is selected, authentik automatically redirects the user to that source. The fuzzer MUST expect this auto-redirect behavior and not treat the absence of an intermediate identifier step as flow confusion.

Application access in authentik is allow-all when no bindings are defined. For any SAML authorization-binding test that relies on application restriction, the fuzzer MUST bind a policy/group/user to the application or entitlement first; otherwise successful access is the documented default and not an I5 violation.

Application policy engine mode changes authorization semantics: ANY allows any single bound policy/group/user to grant access, while ALL requires all to pass. The fuzzer MUST record and control this mode when testing SAML authorization narrowing or escalation, or results may be misread as overbroad grants.

SAML property mappings are arbitrary expressions that can emit attributes expected by the SP. For I5 tests about group/attribute escalation, the fuzzer MUST treat mapped attributes as administrator-defined output policy. Extra attributes caused by configured property mappings are by design unless they exceed upstream intent plus broker policy under the tested configuration.

For SAML audience/conditions tests against authentik as SP, the provided docs do not explicitly document whether missing Conditions or AudienceRestriction are rejected. The fuzzer SHOULD test both remove_conditions=true and wrong-audience assertions, but MUST compare against a valid control and report only acceptance of malformed assertions, not mere absence of documentation.
saml.source: SAML source/provider docs plus attack-pattern guidance

saml.constraint: The provided documentation does not expose documented REST admin endpoints for creating SAML sources, applications, users, or MFA settings. The fuzzer MUST rely on separately supplied admin API knowledge or UI automation for setup; do not invent undocumented paths from these docs alone.

environment_defaults.api_pattern: authentik REST API follows /api/v3/{app}/{model}/ pattern. All CRUD operations use this pattern with standard HTTP methods (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE).
